man! For Christians it is a matter of course that a belief such
as this violates the majesty of God, and the Christian recoils
in horror from the consequences to which such a blasphemous
doctrine leads. But these errors have often been denounced
in our day and we do not purpose to enlarge on them.
Nor do we need to dwell on the point that nature herself,
just because God is present within her, ruthlessly corrects
these errors. Whenever man forgets the confines which
separate him from nature, when he tries to ascribe to his own
creations the same value as that of natural force and growth,
then nature reminds him ever afresh that these limits
remain, and that the work of man's hand is weak and liable
to decay.
Nature reminds him of this by the mere fact of the passing
of time, of incessant change, through which nature ever
renews herself, whereas man grows old and ceases to be.
She reminds him of it again in that she repeatedly hurls
herself on man's structures with destructive force in events
which we call natural catastrophes, but which in truth are
not catastrophes of nature at all but catastrophes for the
proud edifices of man which violate the sphere of nature.
For nature herself these events are only a powerful demon-
stration of her inviolable, irrefragable laws; for man and his
works they are catastrophes, "for the elements hate the
structures which man's hand has reared"
No! nature resists too close an intimacy such as man seeks
with her. She resists it again in that she remains for man a
mysterious equivocal force. "Mysteriously nature refuses to
unveil herself to the light of day." Man's religious adoration
of the powers of nature constantly runs the risk of interpreting
nature too simply and unambiguously, of idealizing her
falsely as though he saw only her springtime aspect. But is
this the whole of nature, the aspect which in spring delights
us with its sweet charms and its triumphant vitalities? Does
nature not also conceal sinister mysteries? Does not a mere
